summary: HNCP is an extensible configuration protocol for home networks, built as a profile of DNCP. It lets routers discover network borders and automatically configure addressing, routing, naming and service discovery, and it sets out requirements for home network devices.

eli5.summary: When you plug new gadgets into a home network, they can talk to each other and set themselves up, without you having to do it by hand.

questions: how does hncp find the network border
how do home routers assign prefixes automatically
subtitle: How home routers share state so a multi-router, multi-ISP home network configures itself.

tldr.problem: A modern home can have several routers, several subnets and more than one upstream provider, yet nobody wants to configure addresses, borders, names and services by hand.
tldr.mechanism: HNCP is a profile of DNCP, the Distributed Node Consensus Protocol. Routers use it to share small TLV records. From these they find the network border, divide delegated prefixes among links, pick servers for DHCP and mDNS, and publish names.
tldr.outcome: A home with several routers can configure itself from shared state. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8375.

today: RFC 7788 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2016 and has been updated by RFC 8375.

sections.title: What HNCP Is For
sections.content:
The Home Networking Control Protocol (HNCP) serves the IPv6 homenet architecture of RFC 7368. That architecture assumes zero-configuration operation, multiple subnets, multiple home routers and potentially multiple upstream providers offering multiple prefixes. HNCP also aims to support dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6) operation.

HNCP does not invent its own synchronization. It is a profile of and extension to the Distributed Node Consensus Protocol (DNCP, RFC 7787), and shares its state as TLVs (type-length-value records) carried in the DNCP node state. That state is used to find network borders, divide up prefixes, give addresses to nodes, and set up name resolution and service discovery.

The applicability rules matter. HNCP should not carry data that changes rapidly and constantly. For naming, for example, it only transports DNS server addresses and no per-name data of hosts. HNCP routers that are connected only through a non-HNCP router do not end up in the same HNCP network.
sections.eli5: HNCP is a way for the routers in a house to keep one shared list of facts. The list is for slow-changing things, like who is in charge of what.

sections.title: The DNCP Profile
sections.content:
HNCP runs over UDP on port 8231, using link-local IPv6 with both unicast and multicast. The HNCP multicast group address is FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:11. Datagrams whose source or destination is not link-local MUST be ignored, and each node MUST be able to receive UDP datagrams with a payload of at least 4000 bytes.

Nodes use opaque 32-bit node identifiers, and SHOULD pick them at random. On a collision the node MUST immediately generate a new random one. The DNCP hash function is the leading 64 bits of an MD5 digest. Keep-alives are required on all endpoints, with a suggested default interval of 20 seconds, and Trickle timers are suggested with k of 1 and Imin of 200 milliseconds.

Unicast traffic on unsecured links SHOULD be protected with DTLS, on UDP port 8232. A node implementing HNCP security MUST support the DNCP pre-shared key method, SHOULD support the PKI-based trust method, and MAY support the certificate-based trust consensus method.
sections.eli5: The routers talk with short notes on a fixed channel, and they each get a random name tag. If two have the same tag, one picks a new one right away.

sections.title: Interface Categories and Border Discovery
sections.content:
Every interface belongs to a category, which tells the node how to treat it. Internal means inside the home network and the interface is a DNCP endpoint. External means outside it, and the interface MUST NOT be a DNCP endpoint. Leaf is for clients only, and Guest is for untrusted clients, which HNCP routers MUST filter so they cannot reach other devices inside the network. Ad Hoc and Hybrid are optional.

The border is found with a short algorithm that stops at the first match: use a fixed configured category; else if a DHCPv6 client acquired a delegated prefix, the interface is external; else if a DHCPv4 client acquired an address, it is external; otherwise it is internal. These clients MUST include a DHCP user class of the ASCII string HOMENET, and all internal DHCP servers MUST ignore or reject requests carrying it. Anything that answers is therefore external. The router SHOULD wait 5 seconds by default for a lease before treating a newly activated interface as internal.
sections.eli5: Each door of the house is labeled inside or outside. To tell, a router knocks with a secret password. If a friendly helper hears it, the helper ignores it. Only a stranger outside will answer.

sections.title: Automatic Address Configuration
sections.content:
Border routers publish what they learn from the provider in External-Connection TLVs, which contain Delegated-Prefix TLVs. HNCP then uses the prefix assignment algorithm of RFC 7695 to hand out parts of those delegated prefixes to internal links. For IPv6 a prefix of length 64 MUST be selected when one is available, and for IPv4 a prefix of length 24 SHOULD be preferred. Assignments are announced in Assigned-Prefix TLVs.

Nodes also take addresses for themselves and publish them in Node-Address TLVs. An address MUST NOT be used until it has been advertised for at least 3 seconds by default, and if two nodes advertise the same address, the one from the node with the greatest node identifier wins. For prefixes not using stateless assignment, the first quarter of the addresses is reserved for HNCP nodes and the last three quarters go to the elected DHCP server.

When no usable prefix exists, routers can create their own. A router SHOULD create a ULA prefix if there is no other IPv6 prefix with a preferred time greater than 0 in the network. A router MUST create a private IPv4 prefix when it wants to provide IPv4 Internet connectivity and none exists, and it then MUST forward IPv4 traffic and perform NAT. Router creation of these prefixes is delayed by a random 0 to 10 seconds so that it can scan for others doing the same.

Several TLVs carry IP addresses. IPv4 is encoded as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address, and an IPv4 prefix length is the original length increased by 96.
sections.eli5: The provider hands the house a big block of street numbers. The routers share it out so each room gets its own range, and each helper picks a number for itself and checks nobody else took it.

sections.title: Serving Hosts and Electing Servers
sections.content:
Hosts and non-HNCP routers need addresses and routes. Because a DHCP client normally talks to just one server, HNCP holds a per-link, per-service election. Each router announces capabilities called M, P, H and L, and the winner on a Common Link is the router advertising the greatest value for the matching capability. Ties are broken by the overall capability value, then by the greatest node identifier.

  • H: the stateful DHCPv6 server for non-temporary addresses.
  • P: the DHCPv6 prefix delegation server.
  • L: the DHCPv4 server.
  • M: the multicast DNS (mDNS) proxy.

For IPv6, Stateless Address Autoconfiguration is the general mechanism. Each router sends Router Advertisements on client-facing interfaces with a Prefix Information Option for each prefix it assigned. DHCPv4 and stateful DHCPv6 renew and rebind times SHOULD be short, not longer than 5 minutes. Capability values SHOULD be 4, though any value from 1 to 7 may signal a non-default priority.
sections.eli5: When a new gadget asks who is in charge of handing out numbers, only one helper should answer. The helpers hold a quick vote, and the one with the highest score gets the job.

sections.title: Naming and Service Discovery
sections.content:
Each HNCP router SHOULD provide and advertise a recursive name server to clients. It follows the delegations in DNS-Delegated-Zone TLVs, the domain in Domain-Name TLVs and the names in Node-Name TLVs. Each node SHOULD announce a name for itself, and names MUST be unique in the whole network. On a conflict the announcement of the node with the greatest node identifier takes precedence and the others MUST stop announcing the conflicting TLV.

Single labels and unqualified zones get a network-wide zone appended. The default is .home, and an administrator MAY announce a Domain-Name TLV to use a different one. The DNS-Delegated-Zone TLV has L, B and S bits that relate to DNS-based Service Discovery lists.
sections.eli5: Every gadget gets a friendly name, like a name on a door, so you can say the name instead of the number. If two gadgets pick the same name, the one with the higher score keeps it.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The zero-configuration goal usually conflicts with security goals. Border detection cannot be protected by encrypting HNCP traffic, because external routers do not take part in the protocol. The threats include forged uplinks and forged internal status from outside routers. The RFC says to either secure individual links at the physical or link layer, or preconfigure the adjacent interfaces to a fixed category.

Inside the border, unsecured links leave HNCP open to redirection, eavesdropping, spoofing or denial of service. On links where that is not practical and lower layers do not protect against attackers, DTLS-based secure unicast transport MUST be used. HNCP can also manage a Managed-PSK TLV holding a random 256-bit key, from which keys for other protocols are derived, but that scheme SHOULD NOT be used without DTLS because the key could travel in plaintext.
sections.eli5: A house with no locks is easy to trick. The routers can use secret handshakes, and the doors to guests and strangers can be kept closed.

sections.title: TLVs and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA created an "HNCP TLV Types" registry for values 32 to 511, with registration by 'RFC Required'. The initial types run from 32 (HNCP-Version) through 43 (Prefix-Policy), and 768 to 1023 is reserved for private use for per-implementation experimentation.

IANA also registered UDP ports 8231 (HNCP) and 8232 (HNCP over DTLS), and the IPv6 link-local multicast address FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:11, described as All-Homenet-Nodes.
sections.eli5: Every kind of note in the shared notebook has its own number, and the number list is kept in one official place.

items.title: Internal
items.text: Inside the border; a DNCP endpoint. All nodes implement it.

items.title: External
items.text: Outside the border; not a DNCP endpoint. Access to internal resources is restricted.

items.title: Leaf
items.text: Clients only; internal, but not a DNCP endpoint.

items.title: Guest
items.text: Untrusted clients; traffic is filtered so they cannot reach other internal devices.

items.title: Ad Hoc
items.text: Internal, with no assumption of transitive connectivity. Optional.

items.title: Hybrid
items.text: Internal, but still tries to acquire external configuration. Optional.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 when created; ignored when read.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: Priority for electing the mDNS proxy.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Priority for electing the DHCPv6-PD server.

fields.name: H
fields.desc: Priority for electing the stateful DHCPv6 server.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: Priority for electing the DHCPv4 server.
